## Chapter 2

CHAPTER XXVII

TEUFELSDRÖCKH (1901)

Hay's diplomatic triumph in China lifted Adams's spirits, but King's collapse and Hay's failing health darkened the season; meanwhile the magnet on Adams's desk, and the geologists' confessions of ignorance, warned him that the unity he had sought all his life was dissolving into a multiplicity science could no longer pretend to govern.

Inevitable Paris beckoned. More vigorously than in the twelfth century, Paris taught in the twentieth, with no other school approaching it for variety of direction and energy of mind. Of the teaching in detail, a man who knew only what accident had taught him in the nineteenth century could know next to nothing, since science had got quite beyond his horizon, and mathematics had become the only necessary language of thought. Scores of artists, hundreds of chemists, physicists, philosophers, were at work a thousand times as actively as ever before, and the mass and originality of their product would have swamped any previous age, as it very nearly swamped its own; but the effect was chaos, and Adams stood as helpless before it as before the chaos of New York. His single thought was to keep in front of the movement, and, if necessary, lead it to chaos, but never fall behind. Only the young have time to linger in the rear.

Still something remained for education, and as usual the woman helped. For thirty years he had been repeating that he really must go to Baireuth. Mrs. Lodge bade him come, and he joined them at Rothenburg-on-the-Tauber. Thirty years earlier, a Baireuth festival would have made an immense stride; in 1901 the world had altogether changed, and Wagner had become a part of it, as familiar as Shakespeare. The rococo element jarred. New York or Paris might be venal, sordid, vulgar, but society nursed there certain anarchistic ferments, and thought them proof of art. New York knew better than Baireuth what Wagner meant.

Adams had played with anarchy, though not with socialism, which seemed hopelessly bourgeois. The conservative Christian anarchist drew life from Hegel and Schopenhauer rightly understood; he proclaimed that in the last synthesis, order and anarchy were one, but that the unity was chaos. He was bound to accelerate progress, concentrate energy, accumulate power, multiply and intensify forces, partly because this was the mechanical law of the universe as science explained it, but chiefly because a rigorous philosophy required it, in order to penetrate the beyond and satisfy man's destiny by reaching the largest synthesis in its ultimate contradiction. The throb of fifty or a hundred million steam horse-power, doubling every ten years, drowned rhyme and reason. No one was to blame, for all were equally servants of the power, and worked merely to increase it; but the conservative Christian anarchist saw light.

Thus the student of Hegel prepared himself for Russia in order to enlarge his synthesis—and much he needed it. The Czar's empire was a phase of conservative Christian anarchy more interesting to history than all the complex variety of American newspapers, schools, trusts, sects, frauds, and Congressmen. From the first glimpse of the Polish Jew at the accidental railway station, in all his weird horror, to the last vision of the Russian peasant kissing his ikon before the railway Virgin in St. Petersburg, all was logical, conservative, Christian, and anarchic. Russia had nothing in common with any ancient or modern world that history knew; she had been the oldest source of all civilization in Europe and had kept none for herself. Studied in the dry light of conservative Christian anarchy, Russia became luminous like the salt of radium; but with a negative luminosity, as though she were a substance whose energies had been sucked out—an inert residuum—with movement of pure inertia. From the car window one floated past undulations of nomad life, herders deserted by their leaders and herds, wandering waves stopped in their wanderings.

Could inertia of race, on such a scale, be broken up, or take new form? Russia was too vast a force to be treated as an object of unconcern. As inertia, if in no other way, she represented three-fourths of the human race, and her movement might be the true movement of the future, against the hasty and unsure acceleration of America.

He took steamer for Sweden, then rambled northwards through bright autumn till he reached Hammerfest on September 14. It was not the Laps, or the snow, or the arctic gloom that impressed him, so much as the lights of an electro-magnetic civilization and the stupefying contrast with Russia. Where seventy years before a futile Carlylean Teufelsdröckh had stopped to ask futile questions of the silent infinite, the infinite seemed to have become loquacious, chattering gossip in one's ear. An installation of electric lighting and telephones led tourists close up to the polar ice-cap, beyond the level of the magnetic pole; and there the newer Teufelsdröckh sat dumb with surprise, and glared at the permanent electric lights of Hammerfest.

He had better reason than the Teufelsdröckh of 1830. A week before, breakfasting at Stockholm, his eye had caught a Swedish headline announcing an attempt on the life of President McKinley, and from Stockholm to Hammerfest the news came day after day, until at last a journal announced the President's death. To Adams the death of McKinley and the advent of Roosevelt were not wholly void of personal emotion, but this was little in comparison with his depth of wonder at hearing hourly reports from his most intimate friends, sent to him far within the realm of night, not to please him but to correct the faults of the solar system. The electro-dynamo-social universe worked better than the sun.

He wandered south and came out at Hamburg, Bremen, Cologne. A mere glance showed a Germany new to mankind. Hamburg was almost as American as St. Louis. Coal alone was felt—its stamp pervaded the Rhine district to Picardy, the same stamp as that of Birmingham and Pittsburgh. From Hammerfest to Cherbourg on one shore of the ocean, from Halifax to Norfolk on the other, one great empire was ruled by one great emperor—Coal. Beyond lay Russia, and there an older, perhaps a surer, power, resting on the eternal law of inertia, held its own.

As a personal matter, the relative value of the two powers became more interesting every year; for the mass of Russian inertia was moving irresistibly over China, and John Hay stood in its path. As long as de Witte ruled, Hay was safe. Should de Witte fall, Hay would totter.

## Chapter 3

CHAPTER XXVIII

THE HEIGHT OF KNOWLEDGE (1902)

America has always taken tragedy lightly. Three hideous political murders, that would have fattened the Eumenides with horror, have thrown scarcely a shadow on the White House. The year 1901 was a year of tragedy that seemed to Hay to centre on himself. First came the accidental death of his son. Close on this followed that of his chief, "all the more hideous that we were so sure of his recovery." The world turned suddenly into a graveyard. Among the letters of condolence was one from Clarence King at Pasadena, "heart-breaking in grace and tenderness"; King himself was "simply waiting till nature and the foe have done their struggle." "There you have it in the face!" Hay said—"the best and brightest man of his generation, hounded by disaster from his cradle, dying at last, with nameless suffering alone and uncared-for, in a California tavern. Ça vous amuse, la vie?"

The first summons that met Adams, before he had even landed on the pier, was to Clarence King's funeral, and from that funeral he had no gayer road to travel than to Washington, where a revolution had occurred that must in any case have made the men of his age instantly old.

To them at sixty-three, Roosevelt at forty-three could not be taken seriously in his old character, and could not be recovered in his new. Roosevelt, more than any other man living, showed the singular primitive quality that belongs to ultimate matter—the quality that mediæval theology assigned to God—he was pure act. The relation of age to youth, of teacher to pupil, was altogether out of place. The wisest courtier that ever lived, Lucius Seneca himself, must have remained in some shade of doubt what advantage he should get from the power of his friend and pupil Nero, until, as a gentleman past sixty, he received Nero's filial invitation to kill himself. Seneca closed the vast circle of his knowledge by learning that a friend in power was a friend lost—a fact very much worth insisting upon.

Power is poison. Its effect on Presidents had been always tragic, chiefly as an almost insane excitement at first, and a worse reaction afterwards; but also because no mind is so well balanced as to bear the strain of seizing unlimited force without habit or knowledge of it. Roosevelt enjoyed a singularly direct nature and honest intent, but lived naturally in restless agitation that would have worn out most tempers in a month.

The importance of Cabot Lodge hung on his position in Massachusetts rather than on his control of patronage; and his standing in Massachusetts was insecure. Roosevelts are born and never can be taught; but Lodge was a creature of teaching—Boston incarnate. English to the last fibre of his thought, saturated with English literature, tradition, taste, he had the singular merit of interesting. The usual statesmen flocked in swarms like crows, black and monotonous. Lodge's plumage was varied, and, like his flight, harked back to race. He betrayed the consciousness that he and his people had a past, if they dared but avow it, and might have a future, if they could but divine it.

Modern politics is, at bottom, a struggle not of men but of forces. The men become every year more and more creatures of force, massed about central power-houses. The conflict is no longer between the men, but between the motors that drive the men. For history, international relations are the only sure standards of movement; the only foundation for a map.

Hay had become the most imposing figure ever known in the office. He could instruct an attentive scholar as no other teacher in the world could do; and Adams sought only instruction—wanted only to chart the international channel for fifty years to come; to triangulate the future; to fix the acceleration of movement in politics since the year 1200, as he was trying to fix it in philosophy and physics; in finance and force.

Hay's last triumphs—drawing England, France, and even Germany toward an Atlantic combine while Russia alone remained intractable—seemed to Adams the highest reach a scholar of statesmanship could witness, even as he confessed that such mastery only deepened his sense of his own ignorance.
